title: Photography, illustration and video
instruction: Show public life as it happens, and label every placeholder and generated image.
intro: A photograph in Oath & Action is a record a reader can check. It shows people doing public work, and its caption says who, what, where and when, then names whoever made it. This chapter covers how we choose, crop, caption and credit photographs, how a frame holds a photograph’s place until we have one, where the few drawn and generated pictures may appear, and how we make and publish video.

Two public-domain photographs from federal agencies, the same two chapter 01 shows, teach the photograph rules. Until we commission photographs of our own, a frame that says Placeholder holds each one’s place, and a generated picture appears only with its label and never stands for a real event.

groups.title: Choosing and framing a photograph
groups.line: A photograph shows people at public work, in black and white unless its color is part of the record, and its crop and the words around it keep that work in view.

groups.title: The record behind each photograph
groups.line: Each photograph runs with a caption a reader can check and alt text for each crop, and our rights ledger, our record of every picture we use, holds its rights and any consent before it runs.

groups.title: Placeholders and made pictures
groups.line: A frame that says Placeholder holds the place of a photograph we have yet to make, and a drawn or generated picture appears only where the table after Rule 16.9 allows, with its label.

groups.title: Video
groups.line: A video answers one question. Its soundtrack says what the screen shows, a person checks every caption, its transcript holds every word, and it plays only when a viewer presses Play.

rules.title: Photograph public work while it happens.
rule: Photograph people while they do public work, such as a resident testifying, a clerk counting ballots or an official answering questions at a public meeting. Choose the frame where the act and the people it serves are both in view.

Leave raised fists, megaphones, flag-waving, handshake close-ups, people pointing at laptops, the Capitol dome at sunset, protest signs used as a motif, glossy stock and crowds of identical smiling people out of our pictures, because each stands for civic life in general and shows no decision a reader can follow.

text: A picture of a real meeting on a real day gives a reader a place, a date and people they can check against the record.
why.basis: Design judgment, from our fifth edition’s photography direction

correct.caption: The shot list, a brief for the photographs we will commission. The first two rows are the photographs this guide shows. The other ten take their subjects from our fifth edition, each set at a level of government and in a region with our direction for the shot, and a placeholder holds each one’s place until it is made.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.1. Cropped to its paintings and carved panels, the same photograph shows an empty room, so it stands for government in general and records no public act.

rules.title: Show a photograph in black and white, and keep color only where it is part of the record.
rule: Show every photograph in black and white, converted from the color original, unless its color is part of what it records, such as the brown of tap water a resident holds up at a hearing. A photograph kept in color says in its caption what the color shows.
Change only tone, exposure and contrast, evenly across the frame. Leave off tints, color grades, vignettes and every other effect, since each changes how the place looked.

text: Black and white keeps a photograph’s own reds and blues off our page. The Rotunda photograph in color holds red coats and red, white and blue wreaths; in black and white the view’s one working red (Rule 05.3) stays the only red a reader sees. Black and white also lets photographs from different agencies, cameras and years sit together as one publication.
why.basis: The photography direction our founder and editor approved on October 28, 2026, black and white with color where color is evidence; design judgment for the reasons

correct.caption: The Rotunda photograph in black and white, beside a placeholder for the one kind of photograph that keeps its color, a picture whose color is the evidence, with a caption that says so.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.2. A Prussian tint dresses the people at the meeting in our color, as if they belonged to our message, and shows a room that never looked that way.

specs.value: Black and white, from the color original

specs.label: On screen
specs.value: filter: grayscale(1) on the photograph, and nothing else

specs.label: For print or an export
specs.value: A grayscale conversion made from the original file; the page’s 1,200 px copy is for screens only

specs.label: Color
specs.value: Only where it is part of the record, named in the caption

specs.label: Adjust
specs.value: Tone, exposure and contrast, evenly across the frame

specs.label: Never
specs.value: A tint, a duotone in a brand color, a color grade, a vignette or any other effect

specs.label: On Charcoal
specs.value: The photograph unchanged; the caption in Charcoal’s text tokens

rules.title: Crop to keep the act whole, and change nothing inside the frame.
rule: Crop a photograph so the person acting, at least one person they serve and the thing they are working on stay in view at every ratio it runs at. One photograph can serve all five ratios below. Set each crop by hand, then check that the caption still describes what the crop shows.

A mark laid on the picture after it was taken, such as an agency’s corner logo, comes out in the crop, and its credit goes in the caption. A sign, a map or a badge that was in the room stays, since it is part of what happened. Add, move, remove and retouch nothing inside the frame.

text: A crop decides what a reader believes happened. With the residents cut away, an official seems to lecture an empty room, and a crop that loses the official leaves the caption naming a man the reader cannot see.
why.basis: Society of Professional Journalists, Code of Ethics, revised October 4, 2026: “Never publish fabricated content that could be confused with reality.” Design judgment for the ratios

correct.caption: One photograph at four of the five ratios, each crop set by hand. Every crop keeps the official, his hand at work and at least one resident, so one caption serves them all.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.3. The portrait crop keeps a resident and the map and cuts out the official, so the caption names a man the picture no longer shows.

rules.title: Set words beside a photograph, or on a solid panel over a plain part of it.
rule: Set a headline, a label or a logo beside a photograph, or on a solid Charcoal or Newsprint panel laid over a plain part of it, clear of faces, hands at work and signs. Words never sit straight on the image, with or without a shadow or a gradient behind them.

text: Over a photograph, the ground under each letter changes from one letter to the next, so parts of a headline fade for every reader. A solid panel gives the words one ground and a contrast we can measure. Live text also stays text, so a reader can enlarge it or have it read aloud (Rule 19.4).
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 success criteria 1.4.3 and 1.4.5; our fifth edition’s rule

correct.caption: An article opener: its kicker and headline set above the photograph as live text, and the caption under it.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.4. Set on the picture, the headline crosses dark coats and a pale map. The contrast under parts of it falls to 1.0 to 1, and 17 percent of the ground under it measures under 3 to 1. It also covers the people the meeting was for.

rules.title: Caption who, what, where and when from the record, then credit the maker.
rule: Write each caption from the record: the agency’s own caption, our notes from the event or the event’s public notice. Name who is shown, what they are doing, where and when, in that order, then give the credit.
Give only as much as the record holds, so a record that knows only the month gets a caption that gives only the month. Claim no feeling, motive or result that the picture and the record do not show.

text: A caption is the part of a photograph a reader can check, and each of its four parts sends them to a record. A guess in any part gives the reader a fact no record backs.
why.basis: Society of Professional Journalists, Code of Ethics, revised October 4, 2026: “Take responsibility for the accuracy of their work before releasing it.” and “Never plagiarize. Always attribute.” Rule 01.8

correct.caption: Chapter 01’s caption for the Rotunda photograph, with each part keyed in the order this rule sets.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.5. The caption claims anger and a seizure that neither the picture nor the agency’s record shows. The record says he discussed proposed real estate actions with residents.

specs.label: Order
specs.value: Who, what, where, when, then the credit

specs.label: Who
specs.value: Officials by name and role, from the record; members of the public unnamed unless the record names them and they agreed (Rule 16.6)

specs.label: What
specs.value: Present tense, the act in view

specs.label: Where
specs.value: The place, the city or town, and the state written out

specs.label: When
specs.value: The date in words (house rule H05), only as exact as the record

specs.label: Credit
specs.value: “Photograph: John Prettyman, U.S. Army.” for a named maker; “Photograph: Architect of the Capitol.” when the agency made it; “Photograph: Dustin Cathcart, Oath & Action.” for ours; “Photograph: [name] for Oath & Action.” for a photographer we hire

specs.label: Never
specs.value: The website that hosts the file, such as Wikimedia Commons, in place of the maker; a guess

specs.label: Length
specs.value: One or two sentences

rules.builders: Copy the record’s facts into the four parts before you write a sentence, then join them in order and add the credit.

rules.title: Before a photograph runs, record its rights and any consent it needs.
rule: The same rules hold for our founder and editor, Dustin Cathcart, photographing on a phone at a public event, and for any photographer we hire. Check the host’s rules on cameras before the event starts, and photograph from where the public may stand. A public official doing public work may be shown and named with their role, and a member of the public may appear in a scene unnamed. Ask a person’s permission, and write down the answer, before you single them out in a close picture or name them in a caption. A person under 18 may be shown so they can be recognized only with a parent’s or guardian’s permission. Stop photographing anyone who asks you to, and leave their picture out.

Before any photograph runs, give it a row in our rights ledger, our record of every picture we use: who made it, where it came from, the license or permission that covers it, and any consent. Some of this is a matter of state law that differs from state to state, such as recording a conversation’s sound or using a person’s likeness, and this guide gives no legal advice.

text: The Society of Professional Journalists’ Code of Ethics says: “Private people have a greater right to control information about themselves than public figures and others who seek power, influence or attention.” The code also asks for “heightened sensitivity” with juveniles. A photograph of a private person outlasts the meeting, so the permission has to be on the record before it runs.
why.basis: Society of Professional Journalists, Code of Ethics, revised October 4, 2026; Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, “Reporter’s Recording Guide”; design judgment for the record’s fields

correct.caption: The meeting photograph with two markers and its record. The official is named, with his role, from his agency’s caption, and the residents are seen from behind and named nowhere, so no consent was needed.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.6. The caption names a 14-year-old and her school, and the record holds no permission from a parent or guardian.

rules.title: Write alt text for what each crop shows.
rule: Write alt text for each use of a photograph, for what that crop shows happening, in one or two sentences. Leave the names, the place, the date and the credit to the caption, which a screen reader also reads. When a photograph runs at a new crop, write its alt text again.

text: One photograph can run in five crops, and each shows something different. Alt text written for the wide frame describes things a tight crop has cut away.

correct.caption: Two crops of the Rotunda photograph, each with alt text written for what it shows. The tight crop holds the line of mourners, a wreath, a painting and a statue, and no casket.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.7. The tight crop reuses the wide crop’s alt text, so a screen reader hears of a casket this crop has cut away.

specs.label: Length
specs.value: One or two sentences

specs.label: Says

specs.label: Leaves to the caption
specs.value: Names, place, date, credit

specs.label: Each use

rules.title: Hold a commissioned photograph’s place with a frame that says Placeholder.
rule: Until we commission a photograph, a placeholder holds its place: a frame at the photograph’s ratio and size, with the word Placeholder at its top, the shot it waits for in live text and the caption’s parts still to write. Here a placeholder means that frame, apart from the hint text in a form field.

A placeholder imitates no photograph, so it takes no gray fill, texture, silhouette or stock picture. A published piece with no photograph runs without one, and placeholders stay in this guide, in templates and in drafts.

text: A gray box at a photograph’s size reads as a picture still loading, and our fifth edition’s panels told a screen reader “Photograph” for pictures that did not exist. Words in the frame tell every reader what is missing and what will fill it.
why.basis: The direction our founder and editor set for this edition’s pictures, which asks every placeholder to announce itself; WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.1.1; our October 2026 audit of the fifth edition’s photographs

correct.caption: Two placeholders: a 3:2 frame on Newsprint for an article, and a 4:5 frame on Charcoal for a portrait post. Each says what it waits for in words.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.8. Our fifth edition’s panel looks like a picture still loading, and a screen reader announced it as a photograph that never existed.

rules.title: Label a generated image beside it, and never let one stand for a real event.
rule: A generated image is a picture an AI tool makes from a written prompt. It may serve only as a labeled conceptual illustration, or as the setting around our real work in a mockup, a picture that shows our page where a reader would meet it. Every one carries the words “Generated image” on a solid tab at its top left corner, its caption says what idea it shows and names the tool and the date, and its alt text begins “Generated image”.

It never shows a real person or a real place on a real day, or anything a reader could take for a photograph of an event. Where a platform has its own label, we turn it on too, and we keep the Content Credentials, the data some tools write into the file to say how it was made. Each generated image gets a rights row with the tool, the date, the prompt and the tool’s terms.

text: The Society of Professional Journalists asks journalists to “Never publish fabricated content that could be confused with reality. Clearly label illustrations and reenactments.” The tab stays on the picture when it is shared without its caption, and the alt text gives the label to a reader who cannot see the picture.
why.basis: The direction our founder and editor set for this edition’s pictures, and his answer of November 21, 2026 on generated images; Society of Professional Journalists, Code of Ethics, revised October 4, 2026; each platform’s help or policy page

correct.caption: Where a generated image would sit in a mockup, held by a placeholder: the tab at its corner, the prompt, and the caption that labels the scene and keeps our real page’s own credit.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.9. A generated picture runs with a news caption and a photograph’s credit, so a reader believes a hearing looked this way.

rules.title: Make each video answer one question, from its title frame to its step.
rule: Each video answers one question a viewer could ask, such as “Which age groups reported voting in 2024?” It takes one of two forms, Dustin on camera as host or his voice over charts and atlas views, and it may move between them. The first sentence spoken asks the question or answers it. Every chart on screen carries its source line for as long as it shows.

The video ends on a step a viewer can take, then the end frame. The first time Dustin appears, his name plate reads “Dustin Cathcart, Founder and Editor”. L8, the monogram, signs a top corner (Rule 12.3). Chapter 23 draws the title frame, the end frame, the name plate and each platform’s safe areas.

text: A viewer scrolling a feed decides fast whether to stay, so the question comes first. A video that answers one question can be captioned, described and summed up in one sentence, which its card needs (Rule 16.13).
why.basis: Design judgment; the two forms are the ones our founder and editor chose on November 21, 2026

correct.caption: A storyboard for a one-minute video on chart S04. The question comes in the first two seconds and the step at 0:50. We drew the 0:08 and 0:30 frames at 1920 by 1080 px, with the chart, its source line and the captions, and our exports keep them at that size. The figures are chart S04’s, reported voting by age (Rule 14.19). Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey Voting and Registration Supplement, Table A-1, reported voting by age, and Table 1 with the Source and Accuracy statements, November 2020 and 2024, United States. Retrieved November 6 and 11, 2026. Self-reported voting among citizens 18 and over; margins of error computed by Oath & Action from the constants the Bureau publishes for that purpose.

rules.title: Caption every video, and have a person check every word.
rule: Every video carries closed captions, made from the final script and checked word for word against the final cut by a person before it posts. Captions, in the W3C’s words, are a “synchronized visual and/or text alternative for both speech and non-speech audio information needed to understand the media content”. A viewer can turn closed captions on and off in the player. Open captions are burned into the picture itself.

Upload a caption file, a text file of timed lines in one of two formats, WebVTT (.vtt) or SubRip (.srt), wherever a platform takes one: WebVTT on our own pages, either on YouTube, and SubRip on LinkedIn and X. On TikTok and Instagram, where we found no way to upload a file, turn on the app’s own captions and correct every word before publishing. Treat any automatic caption as a first draft. Burn captions in only where a platform offers neither, inside chapter 23’s caption-safe area, the part of the frame no app button or crop covers, and leave closed captions off that video, so each line shows once. Put a sound that matters, such as a gavel, in square brackets, and name a speaker who is off screen.

text: Automatic captions mishear names and numbers, and a misheard number tells a viewer who cannot hear something false. YouTube’s own help page says “You should always review automatic captions and edit any parts that haven’t been properly transcribed.”
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.2.2; each platform’s help page

correct.caption: A vertical frame of chart S04 with its source line, at a quarter of 1080 by 1920, for a platform that takes no caption file and draws no captions of its own. We burned its captions in from the checked WebVTT file beside it, inside the caption-safe area on a Charcoal band, and left closed captions off. Until chapter 23 sets each platform’s safe area, the frame keeps to the larger of TikTok’s and Instagram’s margins and clear of TikTok’s buttons. The figures are chart S04’s, reported voting by age (Rule 14.19). Source: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey Voting and Registration Supplement, Table A-1, reported voting by age, and Table 1 with the Source and Accuracy statements, November 2020 and 2024, United States. Retrieved November 6 and 11, 2026. Self-reported voting among citizens 18 and over; margins of error computed by Oath & Action from the constants the Bureau publishes for that purpose.

rules.title: Say aloud what the screen shows, and publish a transcript with every video.
rule: Audio description is a spoken account of what the picture shows. Write the script so the soundtrack gives it as the video runs: read each figure and what it measures, say whose source it is, and name what a gesture points at. Where the picture shows something there is no time to say, make a described version too, a second cut that adds the description in the pauses.

Publish a transcript on the video’s page and link it from every post. It holds every word spoken, who speaks, the sounds that matter and what the screen shows that the words leave out, in order and corrected to the final cut, and it links each chart to its table.

text: The W3C’s page “Understanding Success Criterion 1.2.5: Audio Description (Prerecorded)”, retrieved November 21, 2026, notes that “if all of the important information in the video track is already conveyed in the audio track, no additional audio description is necessary.” A voice that reads each chart aloud describes it as it goes, which serves a viewer who cannot see the screen and one who has the sound on and is looking away.
why.basis: WCAG 2.2 success criteria 1.2.1, 1.2.3 and 1.2.5, and the W3C’s Understanding page for 1.2.5

correct.caption: A script that says what the chart shows, with the transcript that follows from it. The transcript links the chart to its table in chapter 14. Retrieved November 6 and 11, 2026. Self-reported voting among citizens 18 and over; margins of error computed by Oath & Action from the constants the Bureau publishes for that purpose.

failure.caption: Fails Rule 16.12. The voice points at the chart and reads none of it, so a listener hears that something dropped and never learns by how much or in which survey.

rules.title: Where a video sits, show its poster, summary and transcript, and play it only when a reader presses Play.
rule: On our pages a video sits in a card: its poster frame, its title as live text, its length, one sentence with what it finds, a Play button, a link to the transcript and a link to watch it on the platform. The platform’s player loads only when a reader presses Play, and the video never plays by itself, with sound or without it.
If the player cannot load, because a reader is offline, blocks the platform or runs no scripts, the card still gives the finding in its summary and the whole video in its transcript.

text: A card that stands on its own serves every reader the player fails, and it keeps the platform’s player off the page until a reader asks for it. Sound that starts by itself talks over a screen reader.
why.basis: The direction our founder and editor set for this edition’s video; WCAG 2.2 success criteria 1.4.2 and 2.2.2; Rules 17.1 and 17.3

Retrieved November 6 and 11, 2026. Self-reported voting among citizens 18 and over; margins of error computed by Oath & Action from the constants the Bureau publishes for that purpose.
